title: Mamluk Cairo
hookLine: former slave-soldiers rule Egypt and build mosques, hospitals and schools

lines: A BOY SOLD FAR FROM HOME.
cards: A boy is sold in a market far from home, somewhere on the grasslands north of the Black Sea, and shipped to Egypt. There he is taught Arabic, the Qur'an and prayer, then the horse, the bow and the lance.
When his training ends, he is freed and becomes a soldier of the sultan. That was the path of the mamluks. Some who walked it became sultans themselves, ruling Egypt from the citadel above Cairo.
And then they started to build. Today: Mamluk Cairo.

teach.b: In Arabic, mamluk means one who is owned. These were children bought and taken from their families. Nothing in today's story makes that good.

What the story shows is what some of them did once they held power. They built. Walk down the old main street of Cairo today and their buildings still stand shoulder to shoulder: mosques, schools, fountains, tombs.

teach.h: QALAWUN: A TOMB, A SCHOOL, A HOSPITAL.
teach.b: Sultan Qalawun, once a mamluk himself, built a complex with his tomb, a school and a hospital, a bimaristan, side by side.
The endowment that paid for the hospital, as historians describe it, was meant for anyone who was sick, rich or poor, man or woman, without charge.
Later, his grandson Sultan Hasan, born a prince rather than bought, built a great mosque and college, with space for teaching the different schools of Sunni law under one roof. Why build like this?
Partly for memory and standing, like rulers anywhere. But there's a teaching underneath, taught in the very schools they built.

A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that when a person dies, their deeds come to an end, except three: a charity that keeps on giving, knowledge that others benefit from, and a righteous child who prays for them.

A hospital is a charity that keeps on giving. A school is knowledge still in use. Men who had once been owned, and their heirs, may well have been thinking about what they would leave behind when they owned nothing again.
Slaves became builders. People still pray in some of those mosques.

how: Muslims speak of sadaqah jariyah, ongoing charity, and some give to build or keep up mosques, schools, wells and hospitals in the hope that the good continues after them.

games.q: you're Qalawun. you were bought as a boy, and now you're sultan of Egypt, with wealth to spend and a name to leave. what do you build?
o: a palace for yourself and your heirs.
a tomb with a school and a hospital beside it.
nothing. you put it all into the army.
games.why: he built a complex with his tomb, a school and a hospital side by side, a charity that keeps on giving.

practice: Think of the oldest building you can get to, a mosque, a church, a library, a bridge, and picture yourself at its door.
Look for what a hurried visitor misses, a step worn hollow by feet, a patch where the stone was mended, and ask what it was built to do and what it does now.
If you pray, ask that whatever good it still does keep going; if not, simply hold it in mind.

wordCard.voice: Mamluk Cairo. The city ruled by former slave-soldiers, who filled it with mosques, schools and hospitals that still stand. Today's words.

carryVoice: Your line: slaves became builders. A hospital, a school: deeds that keep going. See you tomorrow.
